newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi's biggest bank seen going public in time.
newsitem.headline: Saudi's biggest bank seen going public in time.

text.p: National Commercial Bank (NCB), Saudi Arabia's largest bank, is widening its investor base in a move bankers said on Wednesday was the first step towards going public after years of family domination.

An NCB official on Tuesday said the bank was taking its ownership to 20 Saudi investors after the Saudi cabinet decided to change its status from a joint liability company to a Saudi joint stock company.
He said investors would not be allowed to sell their stakes to outsiders for at least two years.
"This is a prelude to NCB going public. I envisage that it will go public two years after the shares are distributed to the new investors," said a banker in Riyadh.
NCB officials were not available on Wednesday for comment on who the new investors were.
Jeddah-based NCB is the biggest privately-owned bank in Saudi Arabia, with net income climbing to 915 million riyals ($244 million) in 1996 compared to 700.3 million in 1995.
Saudi billionaire Sheikh Khalid bin Mahfouz last July finalised a deal to take over NCB, previously controlled by his family. He and his wife, Naila Abdul-Aziz Kaaki, own the bank.
Mahfouz was made general manager and chairman.
He had resigned as NCB's general manager in 1991 after central banks closed Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), in which he had been a customer and investor.
Bank liquidators had alleged that Mahfouz and an associate were involved in covering up the BCCI scandal involving massive and widespread fraud and other banking violations.
Under a 1995 Luxembourg court settlement, Mahfouz agreed to pay $245 million to liquidators, without admitting liability, in return for the lawsuits being dropped.
Bankers said the move to ease the grip of Mahfouz and Kaaki and invite outside investment could help improve the bank's image by making it more accountable.

"The bank has been more forthcoming in recent years. We have seen this in their statements. If this (opening to investors) leads to more disclosure, that's all for the better. It is a step in the right direction," said an economist.
Bankers said more investors were unlikely to have an immediate impact on NCB's market share, stressing that it was already a major player in oil giant Saudi Arabia.
"NCB already has a lot of the business. Maybe they want to expand in different areas but I don't think there will be significant changes in terms of the market," said one.
But he said that the bank seemed destined to extend its reach to the Saudi stock market, a move that could give it greater exposure.

"It is strange that Saudi Arabia's biggest bank is not public and others are. I think this means eventually it will no longer be the odd man out. It could also increase its visibility in the international banking community."
Saudi Arabia has said it is moving cautiously to open its bourse to foreign investors.
The economist said it was too early to tell whether the latest developments would usher in any major strategy changes for NCB.
"We still have to wait and see. There are several ways to look at it. If there is more disclosure that means there is more chance of it going to the stock market," he said.
"The Saudi market is seeing good recovery and there may well be an opportunity to take the company public. It all depends on the bank's performance," he added.
